name: Ca-AKG

grade_reasons: Imprecision: modest verified sample (~120 participants); effect estimate may be unstable.
Inconsistency: only one study addresses this outcome; consistency cannot be assessed.

layers.note: Human evidence present: human certainty sets the overall score.

studies.title: Alpha-ketoglutarate supplementation and BiologicaL agE in middle-aged adults (ABLE)-intervention study protocol.

claims.summary: For muscle strength, Ca-AKG has only preliminary or animal evidence (1 studies).

honesty_note: No outcomes reached the well-established tier — human evidence is limited. Some outcomes show promising mechanistic or animal data (see 'promising'), but this is not proof of a human effect.

explanation.what_it_is: Calcium alpha-ketoglutarate (Ca-AKG) is a salt form of alpha-ketoglutarate, a naturally occurring intermediate in cellular energy metabolism. It is being explored as a longevity compound based on its role in the citric acid cycle and potential effects on aging-related processes.
explanation.how_it_works: Alpha-ketoglutarate (AKG) is a key molecule in mitochondrial metabolism that helps cells generate energy and remove nitrogen waste. By supplementing Ca-AKG, the idea is to boost cellular energy production and support metabolic processes that may decline with age. The compound may also influence histone and DNA modifications involved in gene expression, which are thought to play a role in aging. However, how much oral Ca-AKG actually reaches cells and exerts these effects in humans remains unclear.

promising_benefits.note: One small human study suggests a potential effect on muscle strength, but more research is needed to confirm whether this is real or consistent.

explanation.emerging_research: Animal studies and laboratory research suggest Ca-AKG may support mitochondrial function, immune cell activity, and cellular stress resistance—mechanisms relevant to aging. Recent work has also explored its potential effects on longevity pathways and collagen synthesis. These directions are promising but remain early; human evidence is very limited and mostly confined to single small trials.
explanation.caveats: Ca-AKG is not yet an established human treatment for aging or muscle health; current evidence is sparse and preliminary. Quality and bioavailability of supplements vary, and long-term safety in humans has not been thoroughly studied.
